You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Babel / Babylon

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, Babel/Babylon functions as the archetypal symbol of human pride, self-exaltation, and organized rebellion against God — the 'city of man' or godless world system standing in deliberate contrast to the city of God (Jerusalem/Zion). Babel represents humanity's attempt to make a name for itself and reach heaven by its own power (resulting in confusion and scattering), and Babylon extends this into the image of an idolatrous, oppressive, seductive world power destined for divine judgment. In Revelation, 'Babylon the great' is the culminating symbol of this anti-God civilization, whose fall is contrasted with the descent of the New Jerusalem.",

    "Genesis 11:1–9 (the Tower of Babel: 'let us make a name for ourselves')",
    "Genesis 10:8–10 (Nimrod and the founding of Babel)",
    "Isaiah 13–14 (oracle against Babylon; the taunt against its proud king)",
    "Isaiah 21:9 ('Fallen, fallen is Babylon')",
    "Isaiah 47 (Babylon as the arrogant, humiliated queen)",
    "Jeremiah 50–51 (judgment on Babylon; 'flee from the midst of Babylon')",
    "Daniel 1–5 (Babylon as the proud empire humbled; Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, the writing on the wall)",
    "2 Kings 24–25 / Psalm 137 (Babylon as the power of exile and oppression)",
    "Revelation 14:8; 16:19; 17:1–18; 18:1–24 (Babylon the great, mother of harlots; her fall)",
    "1 Peter 5:13 (the church 'in Babylon,' widely read as symbolic)",
    "Revelation 21–22 (New Jerusalem as the deliberate counter-image)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [

        "Revelation 17:9,18",
        "1 Peter 5:13",
        "Revelation 18 (commerce and empire imagery)"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Babylon as the end-time or trans-historical 'world system' — a recurring/eschatological economic, political, and religious order opposed to God, not tied to any single city (common in evangelical and idealist interpretation, often combined with the primary meaning).",

        "Revelation 17–18",
        "Genesis 11:1–9",

    {
      "meaning": "Babylon as the Roman Catholic Church / papacy — the classic historicist Protestant identification (Luther, Reformation-era polemic; retained in some traditions such as Seventh-day Adventism).",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 17:1–6",
        "Revelation 18:4 ('come out of her, my people')"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {

      "basis": [
        "Revelation 17–18",

        "Jeremiah 50–51 read as unfulfilled"

        "1 Peter 5:13"

      "prominence": "rare"

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is unusually strong cross-traditional agreement on the core symbolism: Babel/Babylon = human pride, idolatrous empire, and the anti-God 'city of man' set against God's city, drawn from Augustine's two-cities framework onward. Disagreement is concentrated almost entirely on the referent of 'Babylon' in Revelation (Rome, Jerusalem, papacy, end-time system, literal rebuilt city), not on the underlying symbolic meaning. The Rome identification is dominant in academic scholarship, while the trans-historical world-system reading is dominant in popular preaching; these are usually treated as compatible layers rather than rivals."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The self-made kingdom that builds a name against heaven — an empire raised over many kingdoms, the covenant counterfeit.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Gen 11:4; Jer 51:7; Rev 18:10) · see The Bow, ch. 44, and The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Genesis 11:4 — And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
Jeremiah 51:7 — Babylon hath been a golden cup in the LORD'S hand, that made all the earth drunken: the nations have drunken of her wine; therefore the nations are mad.
Revelation 18:10 — Standing afar off for the fear of her torment, saying, Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
